learningObjectives.title: The beginnings of change: the impact of the Renaissance on Britain
A revolution in medicine: Germ Theory and the development of surgery
Modern medicine: treatment, surgery and the prevention of disease

questions.q: The Theory of the Four Humours, which dominated medieval medicine, originated with which ancient Greek physician?
options: Hippocrates
Andreas Vesalius
Louis Pasteur
Ambroise Pare
questions.explain: Hippocrates first set out the Theory of the Four Humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile).

questions.q: Which Islamic physician wrote The Canon of Medicine, a textbook used in European universities for centuries?
options: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
Rhazes (al-Razi)
Galen
William Harvey
questions.explain: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine became a standard medical reference across Europe and the Islamic world.

questions.q: Why did the medieval Church support the ideas of Galen?
options: Galen's belief that the body was designed by a creator fitted Christian teaching
Galen had proved that germs caused disease
Galen rejected all forms of religion
Galen had invented vaccination against smallpox
questions.explain: Galen's idea of a purposeful, created body suited Christian belief, so the Church promoted his work and discouraged challenges to it.

questions.q: Which factor most held back medical progress in the medieval period?
options: The Church discouraged dissection and promoted Galen's ideas as unchallengeable
Governments funded large-scale scientific research
Doctors carried out frequent human dissections
Antibiotics were widely available to treat infection
questions.explain: Church control of learning and its backing of Galen limited new discoveries and dissection throughout the Middle Ages.

questions.q: A person catches the plague in England in 1348. Based on medieval beliefs, which treatment would they most likely have been given?
options: Prayer, bleeding and purging to rebalance the humours
A course of penicillin
A smallpox vaccination
Antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid
questions.explain: Medieval treatment mixed religious remedies with humoural methods such as bloodletting and purging, none of which cured plague.

questions.q: In his 1543 book On the Fabric of the Human Body, Andreas Vesalius mainly achieved what?
options: He corrected several of Galen's mistakes about human anatomy
He discovered the circulation of the blood
He introduced antiseptic surgery
He proved the Germ Theory of disease
questions.explain: Vesalius's detailed dissections revealed and corrected errors in Galen's anatomy, such as the structure of the jaw and sternum.

questions.q: Why was Ambroise Pare's use of ligatures to tie off blood vessels significant?
options: It was less painful than sealing wounds with a hot iron or boiling oil
It completely removed the risk of all surgical infection
It allowed operations to be carried out with no bleeding at all
It proved that microbes caused disease
questions.explain: Ligatures and his soothing ointment were gentler than cauterisation, marking an important improvement in surgical treatment.

questions.q: William Harvey's key discovery, published in 1628, was that:
options: Blood circulates around the body, pumped by the heart
The body is composed of four humours
Germs in the air cause disease
Vaccination can prevent smallpox
questions.explain: Harvey proved the heart acts as a pump circulating blood, disproving Galen's idea that the liver constantly made new blood.

questions.q: Why was Vesalius's work important for the future of medicine?
options: It encouraged doctors to base anatomy on dissection and observation rather than blindly trusting Galen
It immediately produced cures for infectious diseases
It ended the use of the Four Humours overnight
It led directly to the creation of the NHS
questions.explain: By showing Galen could be wrong, Vesalius promoted first-hand observation as the basis of medical knowledge.

questions.q: A wealthy patient in 1550 reads Vesalius's new anatomy book. What impact would this most likely have had on the treatment they received?
options: Little immediate improvement, as better anatomical knowledge did not yet lead to new cures
They would be cured of infectious disease using antibiotics
They would be given a vaccination against disease
Surgeons could now perform completely pain-free operations
questions.explain: Renaissance advances improved understanding of the body but had little short-term effect on everyday treatment of disease.

questions.q: What did Louis Pasteur's Germ Theory, published in 1861, argue?
options: Microbes (germs) in the air caused decay and disease
Disease was caused by an imbalance of the four humours
Bad air (miasma) was the sole cause of all disease
Disease was sent by God as a punishment
questions.explain: Pasteur showed that microbes caused decay, providing the basis of the Germ Theory of disease.

questions.q: Robert Koch is best known for which achievement?
options: Identifying the specific bacteria that cause particular diseases, such as anthrax and tuberculosis
Discovering the circulation of the blood
Inventing chloroform as an anaesthetic
Setting up the National Health Service
questions.explain: Koch developed methods to isolate and identify the individual microbes responsible for specific diseases.

questions.q: Why was John Snow's investigation of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak significant?
options: It provided strong evidence that cholera was spread through contaminated water, not bad air
It proved the Theory of the Four Humours to be correct
It led immediately to the discovery of penicillin
It showed cholera was caused by an imbalance of humours
questions.explain: By linking cases to one water pump, Snow gave powerful evidence that cholera was waterborne, supporting public health reform.

questions.q: Which anaesthetic did James Simpson discover could be used in surgery in 1847?
options: Chloroform
Penicillin
Carbolic acid
Salvarsan 606
questions.explain: Simpson found chloroform to be an effective anaesthetic, later made respectable when Queen Victoria used it in childbirth.

questions.q: How did Joseph Lister's use of carbolic acid from the 1860s reduce deaths from surgery?
options: It killed microbes on wounds and instruments, cutting post-operative infection
It put patients to sleep during operations
It removed the need for surgery altogether
It rebalanced the patient's four humours
questions.explain: Inspired by Pasteur, Lister used carbolic acid as an antiseptic to destroy germs and sharply reduce infection deaths.

questions.q: Why did death rates from surgery initially rise in the so-called 'Black Period of Surgery' after anaesthetics were introduced?
options: Surgeons attempted longer, deeper operations without yet controlling infection or blood loss
Anaesthetics were poisonous and directly killed most patients
Surgeons stopped operating on patients altogether
Antibiotics had made bacteria resistant to treatment
questions.explain: Pain-free surgery encouraged more ambitious operations, but infection and bleeding were not yet controlled, so deaths rose.

questions.q: A hospital in the 1880s wants to apply the lessons of Germ Theory to reduce deaths after operations. Which action would best reflect this?
options: Sterilising instruments and using antiseptic methods to kill microbes
Bleeding patients to rebalance their humours
Bathing wounds in boiling oil
Applying leeches to draw out bad blood
questions.explain: Germ Theory implied that killing or excluding microbes through antiseptic and aseptic methods would prevent deadly infection.

questions.q: Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796 using material taken from which disease?
options: Cowpox
Measles
Bubonic plague
Typhoid
questions.explain: Jenner used matter from cowpox sores to give protection against smallpox, creating the first vaccination.

questions.q: What was the difference between the roles of Alexander Fleming and of Florey and Chain in the development of penicillin?
options: Fleming first observed penicillin's effect; Florey and Chain developed ways to purify and mass-produce it
Fleming mass-produced penicillin while Florey and Chain first discovered it
All three worked together in 1928 to inject the first patient
Fleming invented antiseptic surgery while Florey discovered anaesthetics
questions.explain: Fleming noticed penicillin's antibacterial effect in 1928, but Florey and Chain later turned it into a usable, mass-produced drug.

questions.q: The 1942 Beveridge Report identified 'five giants' to be defeated. Which later reform most directly tackled the giant of 'Disease'?
options: The creation of the National Health Service in 1948
The building of new council houses
The introduction of free secondary education
The payment of unemployment benefit
questions.explain: The NHS, launched in 1948 under Aneurin Bevan, provided healthcare free at the point of use to combat 'Disease'.
